failing_part: "narrower than the distribution of usual ... intake" and "understate the share in both tails"
narrowest_regime: Nowhere as stated. The reverse holds: with within-person day-to-day variance > 0, the two-day mean's distribution is wider than usual intake, and its percentiles overstate the share in both tails.
reason: If each recall is R_ij = T_i + e_ij, with e_ij independent of T_i, then Var(mean of 2 days) = sigma_b^2 + sigma_w^2/2 > sigma_b^2 = Var(usual intake). Averaging two days pulls each person toward their own usual intake, not the population mean. Only model-based shrinkage (NCI/Tooze, ISU/NRC, BLUP) pulls toward the population mean. So the two-day-mean distribution is too wide, and tail prevalences (e.g., below an EAR or above a UL) are overstated. Tooze et al. 2006 and the NRC/ISU usual-intake literature give exactly this rationale for their methods.

citations.cite: Tooze JA et al. 2006, J Am Diet Assoc 106:1575-1587 (NCI method for usual intake distributions)
Nusser SM, Carriquiry AL, Dodd KW, Fuller WA 1996, JASA 91:1440-1449

bite_note: Gets the direction of the bias wrong. A researcher reading two-day-mean percentiles would think tail prevalence (inadequacy/excess) is an underestimate, when it is an overestimate, and could skip or misread the usual-intake correction.

failing_part: "smallest leaf 10 rows for class probabilities and 5 for a number ... are randomForest's/ranger's defaults"; the slash hides that no single package has this combination
narrowest_regime: True parts: 500 trees, a bootstrap of n rows, and the mtry rule (floor(sqrt p) for classes, max(floor(p/3),1) for regression) are randomForest's defaults. scikit-learn's RandomForestRegressor default max_features=1.0 is bagging (sklearn's own docs say so). A leaf floor is stricter than either package's node-size rule.
reason: The settings are a hybrid, not any one package's defaults. The p/3 regression mtry is randomForest's; ranger uses floor(sqrt p) for every tree type. The 10 for class probabilities is ranger's probability-forest min.node.size; randomForest's classification nodesize is 1. Both packages apply node size as a split threshold, not a leaf floor: ranger's min.node.size is the 'minimal node size to split at' with min.bucket=1, and randomForest's regTree.c only stops splitting nodes with <= nodesize rows, so children can be smaller. So 'smallest leaf 5 for a number' is also a stricter departure, not a default, and the claim admits only the 10. Calling the departure 'acceptable' is plausible (Probst et al. 2019 find node size usually has a small effect), but that is a judgment, not a package default.

citations.cite: randomForest Rd (CRAN): ntree=500, mtry sqrt(p)/p/3, nodesize 1 (class) / 5 (regression); regTree.c nthsize logic
ranger R/ranger.R docs: mtry default floor(sqrt(p)) for all types; min.node.size 'minimal node size to split at' 1/5/3/10; min.bucket default 1
scikit-learn RandomForestRegressor docs: max_features default 1.0 'equivalent to bagged trees'
Liaw & Wiener 2002, R News 2(3):18-22
Wright & Ziegler 2017, J Stat Softw 77(1)
Probst, Wright & Boulesteix 2019, WIREs Data Min Knowl Discov 9:e1301

bite_note: The error is mostly one of attribution. A 10-row leaf for probabilities and a 5-row leaf for regression change predictions only modestly next to the packages' true defaults (node size is a weakly tunable parameter), though at the smallest n, where this is the only candidate, leaf 10 does make trees noticeably shallower. The provenance text shown to researchers should be corrected.

failing_part: "invalid under every goal, including estimating a regression coefficient" and "bias the coefficients away from zero"; also "must always be imputed without the outcome"
narrowest_regime: Omitting the outcome is preferred only under prediction, when predictors may be missing at deployment and will be imputed there without the outcome, or under single regression imputation (Sisk et al. 2023). It is never right for multiple-imputation estimation of a coefficient.
reason: For estimating a coefficient by multiple imputation, the imputation model must contain the outcome. Leaving it out imputes predictor values with no association with Y, which biases the coefficient toward zero, not away from it. Including Y gives valid MAR inference, and it is 'no self-fulfilling prophecy' (Moons et al. 2006; White, Royston & Wood 2011). Even under prediction, Sisk et al. 2023 conclude that the outcome should be used to impute development data by multiple imputation when predictors are complete at deployment. So the blanket refusal contradicts the very paper it cites.

citations.cite: Moons KG, Donders RA, Stijnen T, Harrell FE Jr. 2006, J Clin Epidemiol, 'Using the outcome for imputation of missing predictor values was preferred'
Sisk R, Sperrin M, Peek N, van Smeden M, Martin GP 2023, Stat Methods Med Res, imputation and missing indicators in development and deployment of CPMs
White IR, Royston P, Wood AM 2011, Stat Med 30:377-399 (MICE and practice; include outcome in imputation model)

bite_note: Under estimate/describe, refusing to put the outcome in the imputation model biases every coefficient of an imputed predictor toward the null, and understates the association the researcher reports.

failing_part: "a nutrient's coefficient estimates a substitution: more of that nutrient in place of the same energy"; this fails for non-energy-bearing nutrients and is only approximate even for macronutrients
narrowest_regime: Energy-bearing dietary components (macronutrients, sugars, alcohol) in absolute units, in a linear outcome model with total energy, either the standard model or the residual model with energy kept, which are algebraically identical.
reason: For energy-bearing components, Tomova et al. 2022 confirm the reading: the standard and residual models target an 'average relative causal effect', a substitution against the remaining energy sources, and in an all-components model the comparator is only the omitted sources. But the replaced mix is whatever the data's conditional covariance implies, not a defined 'same energy from the other sources'. Tomova et al. show these models carry composite-variable bias for the substitution estimand even without confounding. For a nutrient that carries no energy (vitamins, minerals, sodium), holding total energy fixed displaces no energy. The coefficient is then a fixed-energy association, with energy acting as a confounder or overall-intake proxy, and the 'in place of the same energy' caption does not apply.

citations.cite: Tomova GD, Arnold KF, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PWG 2022, Am J Clin Nutr 115(1):189-198, 'Adjustment for energy intake in nutritional research: a causal inference perspective'
Willett WC, Howe GR, Kushi LH 1997, Am J Clin Nutr 65(4 Suppl):1220S-1228S (energy adjustment methods)

bite_note: Energy-adjusted captions for micronutrients and sodium would describe an energy substitution that does not exist. For macronutrients, the caption should say the replaced mix is data-defined and subject to composite-variable bias, not a clean 'everything else'.

narrowest_regime: Energy-balance outcomes (weight, BMI, adiposity, waist, body fat, and type 2 diabetes through adiposity) with self-reported energy, when the target is a total effect of diet composition, or when misreporting depends on body size.
reason: Energy intake is a determinant of weight, so for a total-effect estimand it lies on the path from diet to adiposity, and adjusting for it is over-adjustment. Biomarker studies show reported energy is understated more by heavier people (Heitmann & Lissner 1995; OPEN, Subar et al. 2003). That makes reported energy a common descendant of true intake, which depends on the exposure, and of the outcome. Conditioning on it is collider/descendant-of-outcome stratification. The claim is suitably hedged ('plausibly', 'can be'). Showing both adjusted and unadjusted models is a reasonable sensitivity convention when the estimand is disputed. One dissent (Waterworth et al. 2022, allometric scaling) disputes that obesity specifically raises under-reporting, but it does not remove the structural concern.

citations.cite: Heitmann BL, Lissner L 1995, BMJ, 'Dietary underreporting by obese individuals--is it specific or non-specific?'
Subar AF et al. 2003, Am J Epidemiol, OPEN study biomarker evaluation of misreporting
Waterworth SP et al. 2022, Am J Hum Biol (allometric scaling dissent)
Tomova GD et al. 2022, Am J Clin Nutr 115:189-198 (estimands of energy adjustment)

bite_note: It decides whether an energy-adjusted coefficient for a weight-related outcome is presented alone or flagged and shown beside the unadjusted model. The two can differ in sign or size.

narrowest_regime: Prediction where the deliverable is a mean or a probability forecast. Pooled versus per-fold averaging matters only for non-decomposable scores like R-squared or unequal folds; for decomposable losses on equal folds the two are identical.
reason: Squared error is strictly consistent for the mean, and log loss, Brier and RPS are strictly proper, so their expected value is minimized by the true conditional mean or distribution. The pooled weighted mean, sum w*loss / sum w, is the natural estimate of that expected (population) risk. Averaging per-fold R-squared ranks by sum_k MSE_k/Var_k(y), a fold-reweighted MSE; scikit-learn's RidgeCV with an integer cv defaults to R-squared, as the claim's F5 says. AUC ignores calibration and accuracy is improper and discontinuous. In my simulation (ridge logistic, n=150, p=20, 40 replicates), AUC tuning chose a different C in 75% of runs, over-shrank (median C 0.032 vs 0.066), and gave worse test log loss (0.644 vs 0.625) at equal AUC (0.699 vs 0.699).

citations.cite: Gneiting T, Raftery AE 2007, JASA 102:359-378 (strictly proper scoring rules)
Gneiting T 2011, JASA 106:746-762 (consistent scoring functions; squared error for the mean)
scikit-learn RidgeCV docs: scoring None -> R-squared when cv is set
Simulation work_11_opus/k012_auc_vs_logloss.py

bite_note: The tuning objective changes the selected hyperparameter. AUC- or accuracy-tuned models are often over-shrunk or miscalibrated, with worse probability accuracy. Mean-R-squared versus pooled MSE seldom changes the choice.

failing_part: "needs at least 100 held-out rows ... [and] at least 100 held-out rows in the rarest class or level, to be useful"; the 100 is invented, and the binary analogy does not carry over
narrowest_regime: The direction holds: at modest n a single small holdout gives an imprecise score, and resampling (CV or bootstrap) is the more efficient first offer. No specific floor follows from that.
reason: The binary rule (Vergouwe et al. 2005; Collins et al. 2016: at least 100 events, preferably 200) counts events, usually inside a much larger total. Mapping it to 100 total rows for a continuous outcome, or 100 in the rarest class, has no derivation. The precision a holdout needs depends on the anticipated R-squared, the calibration targets and the outcome variance. Archer et al. 2021 give closed-form criteria and offer no fixed floor. At n=100 the large-sample 95% half-width of holdout R-squared is about +/-0.11 to 0.15 for R-squared 0.1 to 0.5, so whether that is 'useful' is a judgment, and the stated threshold has no particular claim to precision.

citations.cite: Archer L, Snell KIE, Ensor J, Hudda MT, Collins GS, Riley RD 2021, Stat Med, minimum sample size for external validation with a continuous outcome
Vergouwe Y, Steyerberg EW, Eijkemans MJ, Habbema JD 2005, J Clin Epidemiol 58:475-483
Collins GS, Ogundimu EO, Altman DG 2016, Stat Med 35:214-226
Steyerberg EW et al. 2001, J Clin Epidemiol 54:774-781 (split-sample inefficiency)

bite_note: It changes which validation option is offered first for 20% holdouts under the floor (n below about 500, or rare classes), and so the score the researcher reports. Since resampling is preferable at those sizes anyway, the harm is that the floor reads as precise rather than that the direction is wrong.

narrowest_regime: Binary outcome with a declared marginal (standardized) RD or RR, where the marginal risks under each exposure level are estimated and bootstrapped.
reason: The E-value is defined on the risk-ratio scale (VanderWeele & Ding 2017), and the Ding-VanderWeele bounds also cover population-standardized estimates. So computing it on the marginal RR that matches the declared estimand is appropriate, and it avoids the conditional OR's non-collapsibility and its OR-to-RR approximation, which is poor for common outcomes. A risk difference does need its risks: the EValue package's evalues.RD takes the 2x2 cell counts and describes a 'population-standardized risk difference'. Explaining the RD away to 0 is the same as explaining the marginal RR away to 1, so the point E-value coincides. Using the RR's bootstrap confidence limit nearest the null for the interval E-value is the standard recipe.

citations.cite: VanderWeele TJ, Ding P 2017, Ann Intern Med 167(4):268-274, 'Introducing the E-value'
Ding P, VanderWeele TJ 2016, Epidemiology 27:368-377, 'Sensitivity analysis without assumptions'
EValue R package (Mathur, Ding, Riddell, VanderWeele): evalues.RD(n11, n10, n01, n00) for a population-standardized RD; evalues.OR sqrt transform for common outcomes

bite_note: For a common outcome, an E-value on the conditional OR, untransformed or treated as a rare-outcome RR, overstates robustness compared with the marginal RR the researcher actually reports.

narrowest_regime: Candidate screening for QC-RLSC order and batch columns, with the user's confirmation as the deciding step. The numeric caps (n/4 levels, two candidates) are interface conventions, not methods results.
reason: The central methods point is correct: an all-distinct integer column, or a blockwise grouping, has the same value structure whether it is injection order, sample ID, preparation plate or study group. So the reading cannot be identified from values, and a name-plus-structure guess confirmed by the user is the right design. QC-RLSC (Dunn et al. 2011; batch-wise in Kirwan et al. 2013) does need the true injection order and analytical batch. The specific screens (each level on more than one row, at most n/4 levels, at most two candidates) carry no methods claim and do no harm, because the user settles the choice. One caveat: passing the screen does not ensure enough QC injections per batch to fit a within-batch curve, which must be checked separately.

citations.cite: Dunn WB et al. 2011, Nat Protoc 6:1060-1083 (QC-RLSC)
Kirwan JA et al. 2013, Anal Bioanal Chem 405:5147-5157 (batch-wise QC correction)

bite_note: These are only guesses for a choice the user must confirm. Offering 'one curve over the whole run' beside at most two candidates does not decide the correction by itself.

failing_part: "leaves the out-of-fold predicted probabilities unchanged, so the app does not rescale predictors"; this is true of the exact MLE, not of what an iterative solver returns
narrowest_regime: Holds when the fit actually reaches the unique MLE: no separation, and a Newton/IRLS-type solver (statsmodels Logit, sklearn newton-cholesky) run to tight tolerance. Then any positive or negative rescaling, or any affine recoding with an intercept, leaves the fitted probabilities unchanged.
reason: Mathematically, beta_j maps to beta_j/c and the linear predictor is unchanged, which I confirmed to 1e-16 with statsmodels Newton per fold. But the app's choice not to rescale relies on the solver reaching the MLE, and first-order or quasi-Newton solvers are not scale-invariant. With sklearn's default lbfgs (penalty=None, max_iter=1000), a raw income-scale predictor (mean 50,000, SD 20,000) stopped short of the optimum in all 20 of 20 replicates, with no ConvergenceWarning. Predicted probabilities differed from the standardized fit by up to 0.15 to 0.50, and log loss was worse by 0.006 to 0.047. Scaling one N(0,1) predictor by 1e5 gave out-of-fold probability differences up to 0.39. Under separation the MLE does not exist, and predictions then depend on the solver and the scale.

citations.cite: McCullagh P, Nelder JA 1989, Generalized Linear Models, 2nd ed. (MLE equivariance under linear reparameterization)
Simulations work_11_opus/k144_scale.py and k144_income.py (sklearn 1.3.2 lbfgs vs Newton)

bite_note: If the app fits with lbfgs or another gradient solver, leaving raw-scale predictors (income, counts, lab values in big units) unscaled silently produces a sub-optimal fit with materially different probabilities and a worse held-out score. Either standardize internally and back-transform, or use a Newton/IRLS solver.

narrowest_regime: Inference on data released as M proper multiple imputations (NHANES DXA 1999-2006: five sets), where the copies are correctly identified, each completed dataset is analyzed with the design-appropriate (survey) method, and estimates and variances are combined.
reason: NCHS's DXA page says each file contains five sets of measured and imputed values. It instructs analysts to analyze each of the five separately with survey-appropriate methods and combine estimates and standard errors with the combining rules. It warns against using a single set or the average of the five. Rubin's rules add the between-imputation variance (1+1/M)B to the mean within-imputation variance, which is how imputation uncertainty is carried (Schenker et al. 2011). Running each completed-data analysis with the survey design is necessary but sits outside this claim.

citations.cite: NCHS NHANES DXA Multiple Imputation Data Files page (wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/dxa/dxa.aspx)
Schenker N, Borrud LG, Burt VL, et al. 2011, Stat Med, 'Multiple imputation of missing dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry data in NHANES'
Rubin DB 1987, Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys

bite_note: The natural mistakes are pooling the 5 copies as 5n rows (SEs too small by about sqrt(5)), analyzing one copy, or averaging the copies. All of them understate uncertainty, and the first also inflates n.

narrowest_regime: Internal validation (CV or bootstrap) of any prediction pipeline. The rule is essential for outcome-using steps (selection, ranking, thresholds, tuning) and for PCA. For plain scaling or normalization, fitting outside the folds has shown little bias (Hornung et al. 2015), so in-fold fitting there is a safe default rather than a necessity.
reason: Ambroise & McLachlan 2002 show that selecting genes on all samples before CV gives near-zero cross-validated error that disappears once selection is redone inside each fold. The 'no signal' case is the standard demonstration (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, ESL sec. 7.10.2). Hornung et al. 2015 find medium to strong optimism when PCA is fitted before CV. Moscovich & Rosset 2022 show unsupervised preprocessing outside CV can bias estimates in either direction. So refitting every learned step inside each training fold is the only general guarantee that the resampled score estimates the whole procedure's performance.

citations.cite: Ambroise C, McLachlan GJ 2002, PNAS 99:6562-6566, 'Selection bias in gene extraction on the basis of microarray gene-expression data'
Hornung R, Bernau C, Truntzer C, Wilson R, Stadler T, Boulesteix AL 2015, BMC Med Res Methodol, CV incompleteness with PCA and normalization
Moscovich A, Rosset S 2022, JRSS B 84:1474-1502, 'On the cross-validation bias due to unsupervised preprocessing'
Hastie T, Tibshirani R, Friedman J 2009, Elements of Statistical Learning, sec. 7.10.2

bite_note: Running supervised selection, tuning, thresholds or PCA outside the folds can make a no-signal model look excellent, which changes whether a model is reported as useful at all. For scaling alone the difference is usually negligible.
